title: Where does a phone battery keep its energy?
question: A full phone battery and an empty one hold the same stuff, so where is the energy?
audience: Curious teenagers and adults anywhere who charge a phone every day, often watching with the sound off at first. Many picture a battery as a tank that gets filled with electricity; they know the words 'ion' and 'electron' from school but have never seen what moves inside a battery.
promise: A phone battery isn't filled with electricity: charging pushes lithium into the graphite, where it is loosely held (like a ball pushed up a hill), and in use the lithium goes back to the metal oxide while its electrons are forced the long way round, through the phone; that flow is the current.

loop.line: That's why / a full phone battery and an empty one hold exactly the same stuff.
loop.picture: The last shot tracks back along the board to section A, which has not been touched since frame 0, and settles on frame 0's framing: the two phones and the '='.

look.mood: The Whiteboard template: one long clean white board (#fbfbf8) with a faint shine and a few ghost marks, flat bright light with a slight vignette, clean, no grain and no glow. Black marker (#1e1e1e) for most lines, even weight with rounded ends and a dry edge, drawn on stroke by stroke at writing speed (ink.js drawOn and write under url(#marker)); blue (#2f80ed) only for the key idea: the lithium ions and the key words; red (#eb5757) only for the warning: the electron the separator turns back. No large colour fills. Hand lettering in Patrick Hand, written on as said. Captions: every spoken line hand-lettered near the bottom as it is said (subtitles), its *key* word in blue; the question in s02 is already lettered on the board, so that shot has no caption. The camera tracks along the one board from drawing to drawing (stage.camx); a drawing is erased with a quick wipe. Nothing moves except by being drawn, apart from the elements that slide to show the change: the ions, the electrons on the wire and the ball on the hill.

music.track: Composed for this film (ElevenLabs Music, music/bed.mp3)
music.note: A light, upbeat bed composed to the take's length: ukulele and pizzicato with a soft glockenspiel and finger snaps, no lead melody, low under the voice; it drops to a thin pulse under the hill (s11, s12) so the analogy lands, picks up as the phone lights (s16) and dips on 'empty' (s17); its tail runs on over the opening so the loop is seamless. Effects per shot, from the template's Sound line: marker squeaks for every stroke and word written (all shots), a tap on the '=' (s01) and the '?' (s02), a plug-in click (s08), light ticks as electrons run along the wire (s08, s15, s16), soft slides and clicks as ions settle (s09, s09b, s13, s17), a rising squeak as the ball is pushed up (s11), a quick wipe of the eraser (s10, s13), a dull bump for the blocked electron (s14), a small chime as the screen lights (s16), and the air of the board tracking by under s19. The cuts follow the take.

facts.claim: Phones run on lithium-ion batteries; the usual phone chemistry is lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO₂) at the positive side and graphite at the negative side. The film calls the positive side 'metal oxide' and writes '(in phones: lithium cobalt oxide)' small.
facts.source: Battery University (Cadex Electronics), BU-205 'Types of Lithium-ion' (batteryuniversity.com/article/bu-205-types-of-lithium-ion): 'Its high specific energy makes Li-cobalt the popular choice for mobile phones, laptops and digital cameras. The battery consists of a cobalt oxide cathode and a graphite carbon anode.' UL Research Institutes, 'What Are Lithium-Ion Batteries?' (ul.org/library/what-lithium-ion-battery-factsheet): li-ion powers 'our mobile phones'.

facts.claim: Inside the cell: a negative electrode of graphite (coated on copper foil), a positive electrode of metal oxide (coated on aluminium foil), a porous polymer separator between them, and an electrolyte (a lithium salt in an organic solvent). In a phone the cell is flat: the sheets are wound and flattened into a roll (or stacked) inside a sealed pouch. Simplification: the film draws one sandwich of three layers and leaves out the foils and the double-sided coating.
facts.source: Battery University BU-204 'How do Lithium Batteries Work?' (batteryuniversity.com/article/bu-204-how-do-lithium-batteries-work): 'a metal oxide positive electrode (cathode) that is coated onto an aluminum current collector, a negative electrode (anode) made from carbon/graphite coated on a copper current collector, a separator and electrolyte made of lithium salt in an organic solvent'; BU-301a 'Types of Battery Cells': prismatic cells 'wound and flattened into a pseudo-prismatic jelly roll ... predominantly found in mobile phones'; the pouch cell; BU-306 'What is the Function of the Separator?' (a polyolefin film, commonly about 10 to 25 µm thick).

facts.claim: Lithium ions shuttle between the two electrodes: on charge from the oxide to the graphite, on discharge back again; in the graphite they sit between its layers (intercalation: about one lithium for six carbon atoms); the electrodes are not used up as they are in most other batteries (a little lithium is lost over hundreds of cycles, f7). The film's six ions are a stand-in for billions.
facts.source: Battery University BU-204: 'During discharge, the ions flow from the anode to the cathode through the electrolyte and separator; charge reverses the direction' and 'It takes six carbon (graphite) atoms to bind to a single lithium ion'; The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2019, popular information (nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2019/popular-information/): 'the lithium ions flow back and forth between the electrodes', 'intercalated in the molecular layers in graphite'.

facts.claim: Charging is driven from outside: the charger's voltage supplies electrons to the graphite through the external wire while the lithium ions move through the electrolyte into the graphite. It does not happen by itself (non-spontaneous).
facts.source: LG Energy Solution, Battery Inside, 'How Lithium-ion Batteries Work: An Electrochemical Explanation' (inside.lgensol.com, 2026): 'During charging ... electrons are supplied to the anode through an external power source, while lithium ions move through the electrolyte and are reinserted into the anode ... charging is a non-spontaneous electrochemical process driven by an externally applied voltage.' Nobel 2019 popular information: 'When he charged the petroleum coke with electrons, the lithium ions were drawn into the material.'

facts.claim: Where the energy is: lithium in the graphite is loosely bound; in the oxide it is bonded much more strongly, so its move back to the oxide is energetically downhill and releases energy, and only a high enough charging voltage can drive it back up. The film's hill is an analogy (gravity stands in for chemical bonding), not a measured energy diagram.
facts.source: S. H. Finkelstein, M. Ricci, T. Bötticher, K. Schmidt-Rohr, 'How lithium-ion batteries work conceptually: thermodynamics of Li bonding in idealized electrodes', Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, 2024, doi:10.1039/d4cp00818a (abstract via Europe PMC): 'compared to loosely-bound lithium in the negative electrode (anode), lithium in the ionic positive electrode is more strongly bonded, moves there in an energetically downhill irreversible process ... Only a sufficiently high charging voltage can drive it back.' LG Energy Solution (as f4): 'Because discharge proceeds toward a lower-energy state, it occurs spontaneously.' Nobel 2019: the ions flow 'towards the cobalt oxide in the cathode, which has a much higher potential'.

facts.claim: The separator lets lithium ions through its pores but does not conduct electrons, and the electrolyte in its pores carries ions but not electrons, so on discharge the electrons must travel through the outside circuit (the phone) to reach the oxide; that flow of electrons is the electric current that powers the device. (The film stops its electron at a pore like the one the ion used, so the block reads as 'not a conductor', not as 'too big'.)
facts.source: Battery University BU-306: 'Although ions pass freely between the electrodes, the separator is an isolator with no electrical conductivity.' LG Energy Solution (as f4): 'the separator blocks the internal movement of electrons, ensuring that current flows through the external circuit'; LG Energy Solution, 'Lithium-Ion Battery's Structure and How It Works' (inside.lgensol.com, 2022): the electrolyte must 'prevent the electrons from entering the electrolyte and make them only move along the external conducting wire'. UL Research Institutes: 'Electrons move in the opposite direction in the external circuit. This migration is the reason the battery powers the device.'

facts.claim: A battery does not store electricity (or extra electrons): it turns electrical energy into chemical energy and back. A full and an empty phone battery hold the same materials and the same lithium; only where the lithium sits differs. Simplifications, kept off screen: over hundreds of cycles a little lithium is lost to side reactions; and the stored energy has a mass equivalent (E = mc²), which for an example 5 000 mAh × 3.87 V cell is 19.35 Wh = 69 660 J, / (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)² ≈ 7.7 × 10⁻¹³ kg, less than a nanogram, far below anything a scale could detect.
facts.source: LG Energy Solution (as f4), Key Q&A: 'A battery does not store electricity itself. Instead, it is an electrochemical system that converts electrical energy into chemical energy for storage, then converts it back into electrical energy when needed.' Nobel 2019 popular information (ions flow back and forth without reacting with their surroundings). The mass arithmetic is ours (the cell is an example, not a claim in the film).

facts.claim: 'Empty' is when the lithium has moved back to the oxide. Simplification: a phone stops at a cut-off voltage (Battery University gives a usable range of about 3.70 to 2.80 V per cell) before every last lithium has left the graphite, and some lithium is never moved; the film says 'once it's all home' and draws all six back.
facts.source: Battery University BU-204: 'the flat discharge curve offers effective utilization of the stored energy in a desirable and flat voltage spectrum of 3.70–2.80V/cell'; the direction of the ions on discharge as f3.

acts.title: The question
acts.goal: Full and empty hold the same things: so where is the energy?

acts.title: Inside
acts.goal: Open the phone's battery: graphite, separator and electrolyte, metal oxide, and the lithium that moves.

acts.title: Charging
acts.goal: Charging pushes electrons round and lithium into the graphite, where it is not comfortable.

acts.title: The hill
acts.goal: The ball pushed up a hill: the energy is in the lithium's position.

acts.title: In use
acts.goal: Lithium goes back; the electrons can only go round through the phone: that is the current.

acts.title: The answer
acts.goal: Charging lifts lithium back up; nothing is filled; then the bridge into the first line.

shots.voice: A full phone battery and an empty one hold *exactly the same* stuff.
shots.teaches: The surprise that opens the question: a full phone battery and an empty one contain exactly the same things.
shots.screen: Frame 0 is finished: a clean white board (#fbfbf8) with a faint shine and a few ghost marks. Two phones seen from the back with the cover off, drawn in black marker: left one with a full battery icon and '100%' above it, 'full' under it; right one with an empty icon, '0%', 'empty'. Each shows its flat battery with a window on its insides: two thin bands and a dashed line between them, and the same six blue lithium ions, in the left band of the full one and in the right band of the empty one. A big blue '=' between the phones.
shots.motion: The camera holds, then pushes in slowly toward the '='; on 'exactly the same' the marker taps the '=' (a squeak). The spoken line is hand-lettered as a caption beside the bottom edge, word by word, 'exactly the same' in blue.
shots.carries: The two phones (section A of the board).
shots.transition: The camera tracks right to a clean stretch of board.
shots.sound: The light, upbeat bed starts under the first word; a marker squeak on the '='.
shots.check: Frame 0 is complete; both phones read as phones; the six ions are the same six in both.

frames.note: Frame 0: the two phones, full and empty, and the '=' between them.

shots.teaches: Look inside the real thing: a phone's battery is a flat sealed pouch.

shots.transition: The camera tracks right along the strip, which grows into a big slice of the cell.

shots.teaches: The thing that moves: lithium, which can sit on either side and travel between them.

shots.teaches: Charging: the charger pushes electrons round the outside wire into the graphite.

shots.teaches: At the same time the lithium ions leave the oxide and cross the electrolyte and the separator.

shots.teaches: The ions slip in between the graphite's sheets and stay there.
shots.screen: Pushed in on the graphite: its sheets drawn as long parallel lines (110 px apart) ending at the block's edge, the separator dashed on the right; blue ions arrive from the right and slide into the gaps between the sheets.
shots.motion: The camera pushes in; three ions slide in from the right and each settles in a gap between two sheets with a small click.

shots.transition: Continuous: a second close-up is drawn beside it.
shots.sound: Three small clicks as the ions settle.
shots.check: Each ion sits between two sheets, not on them.

shots.teaches: A turn: the lithium in the graphite is not where it wants to be.
shots.screen: Up the board above the cell, a clean stretch: two graphite sheets drawn large with one ion between them, 'in graphite'.
shots.motion: The camera tilts up the board from the graphite, staying close; the graphite close-up is drawn as the line is said; a beat of silence after 'catch'.
shots.carries: The ion between two sheets.
shots.transition: Continuous: the oxide close-up is drawn beside it.
shots.sound: A marker stroke for each sheet.
shots.check: It reads as a closer look at the graphite.

frames.note: Tilting up the board: the graphite close-up starts.
One ion between two graphite sheets, in the left half.

shots.teaches: In the graphite the lithium is only loosely held; in the oxide it is held tightly.
shots.screen: Two close-ups side by side: left, an ion between two graphite sheets with room round it and small wobble marks, 'loose: doesn't like it here'; right, an ion wedged between rings of the oxide with short bond strokes to them, 'held tight: at home'.
shots.motion: The oxide close-up is drawn on the right; the wobble marks on the left boil and the loose ion jitters, the right ion stays still.
shots.carries: The idea: graphite is the uncomfortable place.
shots.transition: The close-ups are wiped; the camera pulls back and a hill is drawn beside the cell.

shots.check: The two places read as loose and tight without the words.

Loose on the left; held tight on the right.
Both labelled: 'doesn't like it here', 'at home'.

shots.voice: It's a ball pushed up a *hill*:
shots.teaches: An analogy: putting lithium into the graphite is like pushing a ball up a hill.
shots.screen: Back to the whole cell (charger, six ions in the graphite) and, in the right third of the board, a hill drawn as one marker line: high and flat on the left, labelled 'in graphite', curving down to 'in metal oxide' at the right; a blue ion as the ball, pushed up the slope to the top.
shots.motion: The camera pulls back; the hill is drawn in one stroke; the ball slides up the slope with a dashed blue arrow 'pushed up' and stops on the top.
shots.carries: The hill with the ball on top.
shots.transition: Continuous: the height is marked.
shots.sound: A rising squeak as the ball goes up.
shots.check: The hill's high side is the graphite side (left), the same side as in the cell.

frames.note: Pulled back: the charged cell; the hill drawn.
The ball pushed up the slope.
The ball resting on the top of the hill.

shots.teaches: The stored energy is the lithium's position: up in the graphite.
shots.screen: The same board: a dashed ground line under the hill and, at its left, a measure from the ground up to the top where the ball sits, labelled 'stored energy' in blue; in the cell the six ions in the graphite get a blue bracket: they are the ball at the top.
shots.motion: The measure is drawn up beside the slope and written; then the bracket in the cell.
shots.carries: Ball on top, ions in the graphite.

shots.voice: Now use your phone, and the lithium heads *home*.
shots.teaches: Using the phone: the lithium heads home, back down to the oxide ('home' answers 'doesn't like it there').
shots.screen: The charger is wiped out of the gap and a small phone is drawn there instead, 'phone'; in the cell the first ions leave the graphite toward the oxide; on the hill the ball starts to roll down.
shots.motion: A quick wipe takes the charger; the phone is drawn in its place; two ions slide right through the electrolyte; the ball rolls a little way down with a dashed arrow 'rolls down'.
shots.carries: The phone in the circuit, ions on the move.
shots.transition: The camera pushes in on the separator.
shots.sound: A quick wipe; a soft roll for the ball.
shots.check: The ions move right (toward the oxide), the opposite of s09.

frames.note: The charger wiped; the phone drawn in the gap.
Ions start back toward the oxide.
The ball rolling; ions crossing.

shots.teaches: The separator lets the ions through but not the electrons: the electron is stopped at the same kind of opening the ion used, so it is not a matter of size (the electrolyte and the separator carry ions, never electrons).
shots.screen: Close on the separator, drawn as a thick wall with gaps (pores): a blue ion passes through a pore to the right, 'through a pore'; a black electron dot runs at the wall and is stopped, a red cross on it and a red arrow turning it back, 'electrons can't pass' in red.
shots.motion: The camera pushes in; the ion slides through the pore; the electron bumps the wall, the red cross is drawn and it is turned back.
shots.carries: The turned-back electron.
shots.transition: The camera pulls back to the whole circuit.
shots.sound: A soft pass for the ion; a dull bump and a short red-marker squeak for the electron.
shots.check: Red is used only for the blocked electron.

frames.note: Close on the separator; an ion and an electron on the graphite side.
The ion passes through a pore; the electron is stopped.
The electron turned back: 'electrons can't pass'.

shots.voice: So they go the *long way* round, through your phone.
shots.teaches: So the electrons take the long way round: out of the graphite, along the wire, through the phone, into the oxide.
shots.screen: The whole circuit again: electrons running from the graphite up the wire, through the phone, and down into the oxide, with black arrows on the wire; inside, the ions keep crossing to the oxide.
shots.motion: The camera pulls back; the electron dots run round the wire left to right while the ions cross inside, in step.
shots.carries: The flow round the circuit.
shots.transition: Continuous: the phone's screen lights.
shots.sound: A light run of ticks along the wire.
shots.check: Electrons and ions both end up on the oxide side, by two different paths.

frames.note: Pulled back: the circuit with the phone.
Electrons leave the graphite up the wire.

shots.voice: That flow is the *current* that runs your phone.
shots.teaches: That flow of electrons through the phone is the electric current that runs it.
shots.screen: The same circuit: the phone's screen lights (three blue rays above it), a blue label 'current' along the wire; electrons all along the wire.
shots.motion: The rays are drawn on 'current'; the label is written along the wire; the dots keep running.
shots.carries: The lit phone, the current.
shots.transition: Continuous: the last ions arrive in the oxide.
shots.sound: A small bright chime as the screen lights.
shots.check: The label sits on the wire it names.

shots.voice: Once it's all home, the battery's *empty*.
shots.teaches: When the lithium is back in the oxide, the battery is empty.
shots.screen: All six ions back between the oxide rows (as in s07); the ball at the bottom of the hill; the phone's screen dark with a small empty battery icon, '0%'.

shots.carries: The empty cell: the same six ions, on the other side.

frames.note: The last ions sliding home.

shots.voice: Charging doesn't add electricity. It pushes lithium back *up the hill*.
shots.teaches: The answer in one frame: charging lifts the lithium back up; using the phone lets it roll down while the electrons run through the phone; nothing is added or used up.
